questions.scenario: A training centre stores Enrolment(student, course, campus) as a mathematical relation. Its tuples are (A,SQL,North), (B,SQL,North), (C,AI,South), (D,SQL,South). An analyst projects only course and campus.
questions.prompt: Which conclusions follow under relational-algebra set semantics?

options.text: The projection preserves enough information to count students in every course-campus group.
options.why: Projection removes student identity and duplicate projected tuples; the North SQL student count is lost.

options.text: Projecting campus alone produces two tuples.
options.why: Only North and South remain, each once.

options.text: The two North SQL records collapse because the projected course-campus values are identical.
options.why: Set projection removes the student attribute and then deduplicates the remaining tuples.

options.text: The result has degree two.
options.why: Degree counts attributes, and the projection retains course and campus.

options.text: The projection contains three tuples.
options.why: The two distinct students in SQL at North collapse into one projected tuple.

questions.explanation: Projection changes the attributes and removes duplicate resulting tuples. Distinct original tuples need not remain distinct after projection.

questions.scenario: A company needs the names of employees with salary at least 40000. EMP has attributes (eid, name, salary, dept). A developer tries to move operations earlier to reduce intermediate results.
questions.prompt: Which transformations are valid for every EMP instance?

options.text: Replacing ≥40000 with >40000 preserves the answer in every database.
options.why: An employee earning exactly 40000 is a counterexample.

options.text: π_name(σ_salary≥40000(EMP)) answers the request.
options.why: The salary condition is evaluated before salary is discarded.

options.text: σ_salary≥40000(π_name(EMP)) is valid because salary still exists in the source table.
options.why: The selection receives only the intermediate relation, where salary is absent.

options.text: π_name(σ_salary≥40000(π_salary(EMP))) answers the request.
options.why: The inner projection removes name, so the final projection cannot recover it.

options.text: Selecting dept=5 and then salary≥40000 is equivalent to selecting their conjunction.
options.why: Both selections retain exactly tuples satisfying both predicates.

questions.explanation: An operator can use only attributes available in its input relation. Selection can be pushed below projection only when its required attributes remain available.

questions.scenario: An outreach team wants one relation of recipient identifiers and email addresses. R(id:int,email:text) is compatible with S(code:int,address:text) after renaming. T(email:text,id:int) uses the reverse order.

options.text: Reordering T to (id,email) can make it union-compatible with R.
options.why: The same attributes can be placed in matching domain order.

options.text: R − S requires union compatibility just as R ∪ S does.
options.why: Set difference also compares complete tuples over aligned schemas.

options.text: Matching relation cardinalities are required before a union.
options.why: The numbers of tuples may differ; compatibility concerns the attribute structure.

options.text: R ∪ S is valid after aligning attribute names and retains each complete recipient tuple once.
options.why: Their corresponding domains and degree match; union uses set semantics.

options.text: R ∪ T is valid merely because both have two attributes.
options.why: Corresponding positions must also have compatible domains; here int is paired with text.

questions.explanation: Union compatibility is about degree and corresponding domains, not row counts or merely having similarly named fields.

questions.scenario: A library compares registered workshop members A={1,2,3,4} with members who paid B={2,4,5}. Both relations have one integer member-id attribute.
questions.prompt: Which results or interpretations are correct?

options.why: These are registered members absent from the paid set.
The reverse difference is {5}, a paid identifier absent from registration.
These identifiers occur in both sets.

options.text: A ∪ B has seven tuples because the input cardinalities are four and three.
options.why: Union removes duplicate identifiers 2 and 4, giving five tuples.

options.text: (A − B) ∩ (B − A) identifies identifiers present in exactly one list.
options.why: The directional differences are disjoint, so their intersection is empty; their union is needed.

questions.explanation: Write out complete tuple membership before applying a set operation. Difference is directional; union is not bag concatenation.

questions.topic: Natural join with extra common attributes
questions.scenario: A delivery firm stores Parcel(pid, depot, status) and Depot(depot, status, manager). Parcel.status describes delivery progress; Depot.status describes whether the depot is open. The intended match is only by depot.

options.text: Renaming Depot.status before the natural join can remove the accidental status match.
options.why: After renaming, depot is the only common attribute name.

options.text: Natural join must return more tuples than an equijoin on depot alone.
options.why: Its additional equality restriction can reduce the result; it cannot add matches.

options.text: A natural join automatically understands that the two status attributes have different meanings.
options.why: Natural join uses matching attribute names, not business meanings.

options.text: A natural join may discard a parcel whose depot exists but whose status text differs from Depot.status.
options.why: It requires equality on every common attribute, including status.

options.text: An explicit equijoin on Parcel.depot=Depot.depot avoids the unintended status condition.
options.why: The equality predicate can be limited to the intended linking attribute.

questions.explanation: Natural join is convenient only when every shared attribute name really denotes a required equality condition.

questions.scenario: Three tutors T(tid, speciality) and four rooms R(rid, speciality) have distinct keys. Two tutors specialise in DB and one in AI; three rooms support DB and one supports AI. The planner joins on speciality.

options.text: The speciality equijoin contains seven tuples.
options.why: DB contributes 2×3=6 pairs, and AI contributes 1×1=1.

options.text: The equijoin must contain three tuples because there are three tutors.
options.why: One tutor can match multiple rooms; the join is not restricted to one match per tutor.

options.text: σ_T.speciality=R.speciality(T × R) gives the same matched pairs as the equijoin.
options.why: An equijoin is the corresponding equality selection over the Cartesian product.

options.text: Changing the names of tid and rid to the same name makes a natural join equivalent to the requested join.
options.why: That introduces an unintended key-equality requirement, rather than expressing speciality matching.

options.text: T × R contains twelve tuples.
options.why: Every one of three tutors is paired with every one of four rooms.

questions.explanation: Count matching pairs, not participating entities. Shared join values can generate several tuples per original row.

questions.scenario: For a staffing report, Employee(eid,dept)={(1,A),(2,A),(3,B)} and Department(dept,manager)={(A,Maya),(C,Nila)}. The join condition is equality of dept; distinct identifiers are retained.

options.text: The full outer join pairs employee 3 with department C to avoid NULL fields.
options.why: Outer joins preserve unmatched rows; they do not invent a match between unequal department values.

options.text: The inner join returns two tuples.
options.why: Only employees 1 and 2 match department A.

options.text: The left outer join with Employee on the left returns three tuples.
options.why: It adds employee 3 with NULL-extended department fields.

options.text: The right outer join returns four tuples.
options.why: It returns two matches for A and one unmatched C department: three tuples.

options.text: The full outer join returns four tuples.
options.why: It contains the two A matches, unmatched employee 3, and unmatched department C.

questions.explanation: Outer joins preserve designated unmatched tuples by NULL extension. They do not alter the matching predicate.

questions.scenario: An organisation stores Employee(eid,name,managerID). It needs each employee name beside that employee’s manager name. The same relation must participate twice.

options.text: Project E.name and M.name after joining, with distinct output names.
options.why: Both names become available after the role-specific join and can be renamed for clarity.

options.text: Renaming a relation necessarily changes its tuple values.
options.why: Rename changes relation or attribute names, not stored values.

options.text: An inner self-join excludes an employee whose managerID has no matching manager tuple.
options.why: An inner join returns only matches; preserving such an employee requires an outer-join variant.

options.text: Create renamed copies E and M, then join on E.managerID=M.eid.
options.why: The aliases distinguish employee and manager roles and express the correct direction.

options.text: Join E.eid=M.eid to discover management links.
options.why: That matches an employee to themselves, not to the manager referenced by managerID.

questions.explanation: Self-joins need distinct relation roles. Renaming prevents ambiguity, while the actual predicate decides which roles are linked.

questions.scenario: A payroll analyst has Pay(eid,salary)={(1,100),(2,100),(3,200)}. Under set semantics, the analyst first computes π_salary(Pay), then counts its tuples and averages salary.
questions.prompt: Which statements correctly compare aggregates before and after the projection?

options.text: Aggregating the original Pay relation gives COUNT=3 and AVERAGE=133.33… .
options.why: The original relation retains both employees earning 100, so its sum is 400 across three tuples.

options.text: (2, 150), because the projected salary values are {100,200}.
options.why: Projection leaves two distinct values whose average is 150.

options.text: (2, 133.33…), because COUNT removes duplicates but AVERAGE does not.
options.why: Both aggregates receive the same two-tuple projected relation.

options.text: (3, 150), because the original employee keys remain hidden in the projection.
options.why: The keys are discarded, not retained as hidden tuple identifiers.

options.text: SUM over the projected salary relation is 300.
options.why: The projected input contains only 100 and 200, each once.

questions.explanation: Projecting salary first changes the population being aggregated from employees to distinct salary values.

questions.scenario: Sales(orderID,branch,amount) contains (1,N,80), (2,N,40), (3,S,70), (4,S,70). A manager wants branches whose total amount exceeds 100. γ groups and computes aggregates.

options.text: Both branches should be returned.
options.why: 120 and 140 both satisfy the strict threshold.

options.text: Projecting only branch before the SUM is safe because amount exists in Sales.
options.why: The aggregate input would no longer contain amount.

options.text: Grouping by branch and summing amount yields N:120 and S:140.
options.why: Each branch total includes both of its orders.

options.text: Selecting amount>100 before grouping preserves the requested answer.
options.why: No individual order exceeds 100, although both group totals do.

options.text: Select total>100 after computing γ_branch; SUM(amount)→total(Sales).
options.why: The total attribute exists only after the grouped aggregate is computed.

questions.explanation: Row-level predicates and aggregate-level predicates answer different questions. Filter on a derived total after that total exists.

questions.scenario: A club stores Member(mid,name) and Attendance(mid,event). It needs member identifiers that have never attended any event. Both relations use set semantics.
questions.prompt: Which expressions or claims are correct?

options.text: π_mid(Attendance) − π_mid(Member) answers the request.
options.why: It instead finds attendance identifiers not present in Member.

options.text: π_mid(Member ⋈ Attendance) directly gives members who never attended.
options.why: An inner join finds members with matching attendance, the opposite requirement.

options.text: If Attendance is empty, every member identifier is returned.
options.why: Subtracting the empty set leaves the complete member-id set.

options.text: Subtracting Attendance directly from Member is valid even though their second attributes have different meanings and domains.
options.why: The schemas must be aligned before set difference; the projected identifier relations provide that alignment.

options.text: π_mid(Member) − π_mid(Attendance) answers the request.
options.why: It subtracts every attended identifier from the set of members.

questions.explanation: Translate “never” into a set difference over the same identifier domain. Decide the universe first, then subtract disqualifying identifiers.

questions.scenario: A stock team evaluates π_pid(σ_region="West" AND qty>0(Stock ⋈ Depot)), where Stock(pid,did,qty), Depot(did,region), and natural join uses only did. All conditions are ordinary non-NULL comparisons.

options.text: Apply the two selections separately in either order after the same inner join.
options.why: Conjunctive selections commute when all referenced attributes remain available.

options.text: Filter Stock by qty>0 and Depot by region="West", then join and project pid.
options.why: Each filter uses attributes of only its own input and can be applied before this inner join.

options.text: Project Stock to pid alone before the join.
options.why: That removes did, so the intended join key is unavailable.

options.text: Project Stock to (pid,did) only after applying its qty filter, then join to the filtered Depot.
options.why: The quantity test has already been evaluated, and the join key plus output attribute remain.

options.text: Replace the two conditions joined by AND with OR.
options.why: That admits rows satisfying only one condition and changes the request.

questions.explanation: A safe rewrite preserves both the conditions and all attributes needed by later operators. Early filtering is not permission to discard a join key.

questions.topic: Why difference and projection do not commute
questions.scenario: A transport analyst has R(route,day)={(A,Mon),(A,Tue)} and S(route,day)={(A,Mon)}. They compare π_route(R−S) with π_route(R)−π_route(S).
questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe these two valid algebra expressions?

options.text: The first is {A}; the second is empty.
options.why: Difference first preserves the Tuesday tuple, while projection first makes both inputs equal to {A}.

options.text: The first is empty; the second is {A}.
options.why: This reverses the actual effects of the two operation orders.

options.text: Both expressions are well-defined, but they are not equivalent for this instance.
options.why: The schemas are compatible in both differences, but projection removes the day distinction at different stages.

options.text: Both results are {A}.
options.why: Projecting first loses the distinction between Monday and Tuesday; the projected difference becomes empty.

options.text: Both results are empty.
options.why: R−S still contains (A,Tue), which projects to A.

questions.explanation: Eliminating identifying detail before subtraction can change what counts as the same tuple. Projection does not generally distribute over difference.

questions.scenario: A ticket website retrieves a shopping basket using one unpredictable session token. Each request reads or replaces the whole basket. Cross-customer searches are not part of this workload.

options.text: A key-value store is a plausible fit because the dominant access path is a known key.
options.why: The requirement aligns with direct session-key lookup.

options.text: Choosing a key-value model proves that all future analytical queries will be efficient.
options.why: New access patterns may require indexes, another store, or redesigned data access.

options.text: The basket may be structured internally even if the store exposes it mainly as a value.
options.why: Key-value access does not require the application value to be meaningless bytes.

options.text: The team should evaluate expiry and concurrent basket-update requirements, not only the model label.
options.why: Operational and consistency requirements still determine suitability.

options.text: A key-value value may represent a basket containing several products.
options.why: The application can encode the collection within the value associated with its session key.

questions.explanation: Choose the model from how the application reads and updates data. A natural key-based workload is a reason to consider a key-value store, not proof of universal suitability.

questions.scenario: A museum catalogue has paintings with medium and dimensions, recordings with duration and performers, and manuscripts with language and pages. Item pages normally display one complete catalogue item.

options.text: Every document database must reject transactions by definition.
options.why: Transaction capabilities vary by product; this is not a defining universal restriction.

options.text: The ability to add a new optional field does not prove old application code will interpret it correctly.
options.why: Readers and validation rules must still account for schema evolution.

options.text: A document model can keep each item’s related descriptive fields together despite differing shapes.
options.why: Nested, varying records fit the stated item-oriented reads.

options.text: Flexible schema means a malformed identifier can never harm the application.
options.why: The application still depends on consistent identifiers and validation.

options.text: The team should define required fields and versioning rules even if optional fields differ.
options.why: Schema flexibility changes where rules are managed; it does not remove their need.

questions.explanation: Flexible document structure is useful for varied records, but data meaning, validation and application compatibility remain design responsibilities.

questions.scenario: Investigators must repeatedly find accounts reachable from a suspicious account through up to five transfer relationships, preserving the path and relationship properties. Their data is highly connected.
questions.prompt: Which statements support a careful model choice?

options.text: The requirement can be reduced to independent session-key lookups without considering connectivity.
options.why: The requested paths depend on relationships between multiple accounts.

options.text: Path-query patterns and edge properties matter more than choosing a fashionable database category.
options.why: Those access requirements determine whether the model fits.

options.text: Using a graph model removes the need to control access to sensitive account data.
options.why: Security obligations remain regardless of the storage model.

options.text: A relational solution is logically impossible.
options.why: Relations can represent edges and support traversal; a graph model is a candidate fit, not the only possible representation.

options.text: A graph model directly represents the connected accounts and transfer relationships.
options.why: Nodes and edges match the dominant traversal problem.

questions.explanation: Highly connected path queries motivate evaluating a graph database. Model fit does not imply automatic performance or replace security design.

questions.scenario: An environmental platform receives millions of timestamped readings. Most reads retrieve recent readings for one sensor, and writes dominate the workload. The team is considering a column-family database.

options.text: Data retention, growth and the busiest sensors should be considered before committing to a layout.
options.why: Skew and growth affect the practical performance and operation of a distributed design.

options.text: The heavy-write workload is a reason to evaluate a column-family model.
options.why: The lecture identifies heavy write volume as a common use case.

options.text: Partitioning all readings under one constant key guarantees balanced load.
options.why: A single constant key concentrates the workload instead of distributing it.

options.text: Designing around sensor and time access patterns is more useful than copying a relational schema unchanged.
options.why: Distributed NoSQL modelling is commonly driven by the expected queries.

options.text: Selecting this category guarantees that an arbitrary cross-sensor query will never scan much data.
options.why: Costs depend on the data layout and query path, not merely the category.

questions.explanation: A likely model fit still requires access-pattern and distribution design. Heavy writes alone do not make every key layout efficient.

questions.scenario: Two replicas lose communication. A completed price update is visible at replica A but not B. The service promises a response to every request reaching a non-failing replica during the partition. It allows B to return its older price.
questions.prompt: Which conclusions follow in CAP terms?

options.text: The stale response demonstrates that the stated consistency guarantee is not maintained.
options.why: A read after the completed update can return the earlier value.

options.text: CAP proves that the service can never be consistent again after the network recovers.
options.why: The theorem concerns guarantees during partitions, not permanent divergence.

options.text: Refusing some requests until coordination is restored would be a different trade-off.
options.why: That may preserve consistency at the expense of availability for those requests.

options.text: The service is prioritising availability over guaranteed latest/linearizable reads during this partition.
options.why: B responds despite being unable to confirm the completed update at A.

options.text: The two replicas can both guarantee the latest value for every request simply by waiting zero seconds.
options.why: Zero waiting cannot convey the missing update across the broken link.

questions.explanation: The relevant trade-off occurs when communication is partitioned. Responding from a stale isolated replica sacrifices guaranteed linearizable consistency.

questions.scenario: A stock reservation service must never confirm two sales of the last unit. During a partition, an isolated replica refuses reservation requests because it cannot coordinate with the replica holding the authoritative stock state.
questions.prompt: Which interpretations of the stated CAP trade-off are justified?

options.text: Keeping the server process running does not by itself establish CAP availability for reservations.
options.why: The required operation is refused even though the process is alive.

options.text: It sacrifices availability for some operations during the partition to protect consistency.
options.why: The isolated replica rejects reservations rather than risk incompatible confirmations.

options.text: It sacrifices partition tolerance because the network partition occurred.
options.why: Partition tolerance is about behaviour despite communication failure, not preventing all failures.

options.text: It has proved that all NoSQL systems are unsuitable for inventory.
options.why: The scenario describes a requirement and trade-off, not a universal judgement on database categories.

options.text: Allowing customers to retry after the partition does not make their present reservation requests available.
options.why: Future recovery does not satisfy availability during the current partition.

questions.explanation: CAP availability is a response guarantee for the relevant operations, not merely whether a machine is powered on. Refusal can be a deliberate correctness choice.

questions.scenario: A photo service accepts a profile edit at one replica. Another replica temporarily displays the old profile. After updates stop and communication is restored, replication converges to one resolved profile.

options.text: Temporary stale values automatically prove permanent data loss.
options.why: A stale replica may simply be awaiting replication; permanence has not been established.

options.text: Users may need a design that distinguishes a pending edit from a globally visible edit.
options.why: The interaction can acknowledge the different visibility stages instead of promising immediate universal agreement.

options.text: This behaviour is compatible with eventual consistency.
options.why: Temporary divergence followed by convergence under the stated conditions matches the intended model.

options.text: Eventual consistency promises that every read immediately after an edit sees the edit.
options.why: Immediate visibility everywhere is stronger than eventual convergence.

options.text: The service still needs a conflict-resolution rule if independent replicas accept conflicting edits.
options.why: Convergence requires a way to reconcile competing updates.

questions.explanation: BASE-style design tolerates transitional states, but eventual consistency is not an excuse to omit convergence and conflict handling.

questions.topic: Do not confuse two meanings of consistency
questions.scenario: A team compares ACID transactions with CAP. A transaction checks that every invoice amount is non-negative. Separately, replicas may serve different committed invoice versions during a partition.

options.text: The business-rule check and the replica-visibility guarantee address different concerns.
options.why: ACID consistency and CAP consistency use the same word for distinct properties.

options.text: Both replicas can contain individually valid invoices while exposing different versions.
options.why: Validity against a domain rule does not require every replica to expose the latest committed state.

options.text: A NoSQL product cannot offer any transaction support.
options.why: Capabilities vary; NoSQL is not a universal ban on transactions.

options.text: The team should state the required read guarantee explicitly instead of relying on the word consistency alone.
options.why: Precise requirements prevent an invariant guarantee from being mistaken for a replica-ordering guarantee.

options.text: Passing the non-negative constraint alone proves CAP consistency between replicas.
options.why: A business invariant can hold in both an old and a new version while reads are not linearizable.

questions.explanation: Separate data-invariant preservation from distributed read/write consistency. Neither label by itself establishes every required guarantee.

questions.scenario: An online shop proposes a relational order ledger, a key-value session store and a graph recommendation service. The order ledger remains authoritative for payments.

options.text: The team should decide how changes in authoritative orders reach the recommendation model.
options.why: Derived data needs an explicit update and recovery path.

options.text: The design is an example of polyglot persistence.
options.why: It intentionally uses different storage models for different application needs.

options.text: Each added store can introduce synchronisation and operational work.
options.why: Multiple systems create additional data movement, failure and monitoring responsibilities.

options.text: Recommendations being temporarily stale means the payment ledger must also accept stale balances.
options.why: Different subsystems can have different guarantees and authorities.

options.text: Using several databases automatically reduces all development and maintenance costs.
options.why: Better model fit may help, but integration and operations can also become more expensive.

questions.explanation: Polyglot persistence is a workload-based choice, not a free improvement. Preserve clear ownership of facts and explicit synchronisation rules.

questions.scenario: A school exports Student, Course and Enrolment tables into student documents, embedding course titles inside each student’s enrolment list. Course titles can change.

options.text: The team should choose deliberately between embedded copies, references and acceptable staleness.
options.why: Those choices trade read convenience against update consistency and relationship handling.

options.text: Migration is complete as soon as every table has been converted into JSON text.
options.why: Data shape conversion does not establish correct queries, constraints or update behaviour.

options.text: Read patterns and course-change frequency are relevant to the embedding decision.
options.why: Frequent combined reads and frequent shared updates pull the design in different directions.

options.text: A title change may require updating several duplicated embedded copies.
options.why: Embedding creates repeated course facts across student documents.

options.text: The old relational foreign-key guarantees automatically survive the export.
options.why: The new storage and application design must provide the required relationship checks.

questions.explanation: Migration changes data ownership and constraint enforcement as well as storage syntax. Evaluate reads, updates and consistency together.

questions.scenario: A small analytics team is comparing a serverless NoSQL service with a database that supports documents and graphs. A proposal claims either option eliminates all modelling decisions.

options.text: Serverless deployment can reduce some infrastructure management, but does not remove query and data-model design.
options.why: Operational abstraction does not determine the correct representation or access patterns.

options.text: Supporting documents and graphs makes the second product multi-model.
options.why: The product exposes more than one data model.

options.text: Automatic scaling guarantees that every workload costs less than a fixed-capacity design.
options.why: Cost depends on workload, pricing and access efficiency; scaling alone is not a cost proof.

options.text: A multi-model database necessarily makes all data relationships consistent without any design rules.
options.why: Supported models still need integrity and update policies.

options.text: Governance, access control and data quality remain relevant for both options.
options.why: The lecture identifies increased focus on governance and consistency; neither deployment model removes those needs.

questions.explanation: Distinguish an operating model from a data model. Both serverless and multi-model capabilities still need workload, governance and consistency decisions.

questions.scenario: A university wants to replace a stable reporting database because a vendor advertises “NoSQL scales.” The workload has predictable joins and strict enrolment rules; the team has not measured a performance problem. A separate clickstream workload grows rapidly and mainly appends events.

options.text: Require a measured reason for changing the existing reporting design.
options.why: A migration should address actual requirements rather than assume a benefit from a trend.

options.text: Because clickstream data grows quickly, its retention and query patterns no longer matter.
options.why: Growth makes data access and lifecycle design more important, not less.

options.text: Replace both workloads immediately because the NoSQL label proves superior performance.
options.why: A category label is not evidence that a particular system or schema improves either workload.

options.text: Evaluate the two workloads separately against their actual access and consistency requirements.
options.why: Reporting joins and high-volume event ingestion can favour different designs.

options.text: Include migration, training, tooling and relationship-enforcement costs in the comparison.
options.why: The lecture identifies these as material modelling and operational challenges.

questions.explanation: Choose technology by demonstrated requirements and trade-offs. Different workloads may justify different decisions within the same organisation.
